coachMessages.text: Look at the board. Can you find a four-cell window that already has three Yellow discs and one empty space?

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Movestring: 33201. Show the resulting position. Yellow has three discs in a horizontal row at row 0 (cols 1, 2, 3). Mark the three Yellow discs with 'win' overlays and the empty completing cell at col 4 row 0 with a 'tg' overlay. Legend: 'win' = Three connected discs, 'tg' = Threat square (the winning move).</board instructions>

An immediate threat is any four-cell window that already contains three of your discs and one empty square. That empty square is your threat cell — play it and you win instantly.

coachMessages.text: Threats look the same in every direction — horizontal, vertical, diagonal. Train your eye to scan all four.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Movestring: 644565566. Show the resulting position. Yellow has a diagonal three-in-a-row. Mark the three Yellow diagonal discs with 'win' overlays and the empty completing cell with a 'tg' overlay. Legend: 'win' = Three connected discs, 'tg' = Winning move.</board instructions>

The pattern is identical in every direction. Your eye will naturally scan horizontally first — train yourself to also check vertical columns and both diagonal slopes. A diagonal threat is just as decisive as a horizontal one, and easier to miss.

coachMessages.text: The empty square does not have to be at the end of the line — it can sit anywhere inside the four-cell window.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Movestring: 3334243556566. Show the resulting position. Yellow has three discs in a horizontal four-cell window with the empty cell in an interior position (not at either end). Mark the three Yellow discs with 'win' overlays and the interior empty cell with a 'tg' overlay. Legend: 'win' = Three connected discs, 'tg' = Winning move (interior gap).</board instructions>

When the empty cell sits in the middle of the four-cell window rather than at an end, the threat is harder to spot. The rule is the same: any window of four with three of your discs and one empty square is an immediate threat, regardless of where the gap falls.

coachMessages.text: You spotted your own chance to build — but your opponent already has three in a row. What happens if you extend your own line first?

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a mid-game position (around 10–14 moves played) where: (1) Red has an immediate horizontal or diagonal threat — three Red discs with one empty completing cell that is immediately playable (at the top of its column's current stack), and (2) Yellow also has an attractive setup move — Yellow could extend a two-in-a-row to three-in-a-row in a clearly different column. Mark the Red threat cell with a 'td' overlay, and mark Yellow's tempting building move with a 'tg' overlay to draw the eye. Legend: 'td' = Opponent's immediate threat (block this!), 'tg' = Tempting Yellow build (wrong this turn).</board instructions>

Immediate threats are urgent for both players. Before committing to your own move, always scan your opponent's board for the pattern: any four-cell window with three of their discs and one empty square. A missed block loses the game on the very next move — no matter how good your own plan looked.

socratic.goalPrompt: Red has an immediate threat somewhere on the board. Which column must Yellow play to survive?
